Lesson 1

Meet Claude

Claude is an AI assistant made by Anthropic. You write to it in plain language, attach files if you want, and it answers in conversation. It can draft, explain, analyze, plan, and write code with you.

Good at

Thinking and writing

  • Drafting and editing text in any tone
  • Explaining hard ideas at your level
  • Reading long documents and pulling out what matters
  • Writing, explaining, and fixing code
Check its work

Facts that matter

  • Exact figures, dates, quotes, and citations
  • Anything recent, unless web search is on
  • Legal, medical, and money decisions: use it to prepare, then confirm with a professional
By default

What it won't do on its own

  • Look at the web unless search is on
  • Carry memory between chats unless memory is on
  • Touch your apps unless you connect them

The model family

You can switch models in the middle of a chat
ModelThink of it asBest for
HaikuFast and lightQuick questions, rewrites, summaries, lots of small tasks
SonnetThe everyday modelWriting, analysis, coding, and documents
OpusMore depthHarder multi-step problems and longer projects
FableMost capableThe hardest, highest-stakes work. Includes extra safeguards in a few sensitive areas.

Which models you see depends on your plan, so check the model picker in the app. A bigger model is not always the right pick: smaller ones usually answer sooner.

    Lesson 2

    Prompts that get good answers

    A prompt is whatever you type. Claude can only work with what you give it, so the biggest improvement you can make is telling it more about what you want.

    Goal
    What you want at the end: an email, a plan, a decision, an explanation.
    Context
    The situation and the facts Claude can't see. Who, what, when, what you already tried.
    Audience
    Who will read or use the result. A manager, a ten-year-old, yourself next week.
    Format and length
    Bullets, a table, two paragraphs, 150 words, three options.
    Example
    A sample of the style or structure you like. One good example beats a paragraph of description.
    Vague

    Write about dogs.

    Specific

    Write a 150-word intro for a newsletter aimed at first-time dog owners. Friendly tone, one practical tip about the first week at home, and end with a question readers can reply to.

    Prompt Lab

    Switch pieces on and watch the prompt grow
    Your prompt

    What Claude might write

    Example only, to show the difference. Real replies vary.

    Follow up, don't start over

    Treat the first answer as a draft. Short follow-ups work well:

    • "Make it half as long."
    • "More formal, and drop the second paragraph."
    • "Give me three different versions."
    • "What did you assume that I didn't tell you?"

    Let Claude ask you

    For big or fuzzy tasks, invite questions first.

    I want to plan a career change. Ask me up to five questions, one at a time, before you suggest anything.

    Mark off your materials

    When you paste text or data, wrap it in simple tags so Claude knows where your instructions end and your material begins.

    Summarize the text below in 3 bullets. <text> ...your text here... </text>

    More on this in Anthropic's prompt engineering guide.

    Lesson 3

    Tokens and the context window

    Claude reads and writes in small chunks of text called tokens, and it can only keep so much in view at once. That limit is the context window. Knowing both explains why long chats drift and why big files change how a chat behaves.

    What a token is

    A chunk of text: often a short word, or part of a longer one. In English, a token is roughly four characters, and 100 tokens is about 75 words. Code, numbers, and other languages can split into more tokens.

    Input and output

    Input tokens are what you send: your messages, files, and instructions. Output tokens are what Claude writes back. Developers using the API are billed for the two separately.

    The context window

    Everything Claude can consider at one time: your messages, attached files, its own replies, search results, and standing instructions. It is Claude working memory for the current chat.

    What to do when it gets full

    What you noticeWhy it happensTry this
    Claude loses early details in a long chatThe chat holds a lot, and long conversations can outgrow what Claude keeps in view.Restate the key facts, or ask for a summary and continue in a new chat.
    A very large file makes answers shallowThe file takes up much of the window.Ask about specific sections, or split the file into parts.
    A long answer stops partwayReplies have a length limit.Say "continue from where you stopped", or ask for one section at a time.
    You change topics after many messagesOld material still sits in the window and can distract.Start a new chat for the new topic.
    You hit usage limits sooner than expectedLonger chats and bigger files generally use more of your allowance.Keep chats focused and attach only what the task needs.

    How an app handles a very long conversation depends on the product, so do not count on every early detail being remembered perfectly.

    Carry a long chat into a new one

    Summarize the key decisions, facts, constraints, and open questions from this chat in under 300 words, so I can paste it into a new chat and continue.

    Keep answers lean

    Answer in under 100 words. Lead with the recommendation, then give the two most important reasons.

    Lesson 5

    Files, images, and Projects

    Claude works best on your real material. Attach it to a message, or keep it in a Project so every related chat starts with the same background.

    What you can attach

    • Documents and PDFs
    • Spreadsheets and CSV files
    • Images, screenshots, and photos
    • Text and code files

    What to ask for

    • Summaries and key points
    • Questions about specific sections
    • Comparisons between two files
    • A description or critique of an image

    Good habits

    • Say what you want from the file
    • Point to pages or sections
    • Ask Claude to quote or cite where it found something, then check
    Try this with any PDF

    Read the attached document. Give me a 5-bullet summary, then list any numbers or dates I should double-check against the original. Tell me which page each one came from.

    Try this with a screenshot or photo

    Here's a screenshot of an error message I keep seeing. Explain in plain language what it means and give me the three most likely fixes, starting with the easiest.

    Projects, by example

    A Project is a workspace for one ongoing effort

    A Project holds files and instructions that every chat inside it can use. You write the background once instead of repeating it. Good fits: a class, a job search, a client, a home renovation.

    ProjectSpring semester: Biology 201
    Project instructions

    I'm a first-year student. Explain things step by step in plain language. When I ask a practice question, wait for my answer before showing the solution. Keep answers under 200 words unless I ask for more.

    syllabus.pdflecture-notes-ch4.pdfexam-1-practice.pdf

    Why it works: every new chat in this Project already knows the course, the files, and how you like to learn.

    Lesson 6

    Make things, not just answers

    Ask for a finished piece of work and Claude can produce it as a document, slide deck, spreadsheet, design, chart, or a small working tool. These appear beside the chat as artifacts you can keep, change, and share.

    Request builder

    Pick an output, then replace the [brackets]
    Template

    Edit by talking

    You don't have to start over. Say "make the title shorter", "add a column for deadlines", or "change the colors to something calmer".

    Ask for the format you need

    If you need a particular file type such as a Word or PowerPoint file, say so in the request. Many artifacts can also be downloaded or exported.

    Start rough

    Get a first version quickly, react to it, then refine. It's faster than describing everything up front.

    Lesson 7

    Search and research

    Claude's built-in knowledge stops at a training cutoff. Web search lets it look things up now. Research goes further: it runs many searches and writes a longer report.

    Turn search on for
    • News and recent events
    • Prices, versions, schedules, rules
    • Who currently holds a role
    • Anything with "latest", "current", or "still"
    Search isn't needed for
    • Stable facts and definitions
    • Explaining a concept
    • Editing or brainstorming from your own text
    Research mode

    Use it when you want a thorough comparison or report with sources and can wait a few minutes. Availability depends on your plan and settings.

    Search or no search?

    0 of 5
    Try this with search on

    Compare the three most popular note-taking apps right now. Give me a table of price, platforms, and standout feature. Link each claim to its source and tell me where sources disagree.

    Always check: open the sources for anything you'll rely on. Ask Claude "which parts of this are you least sure about?"

    Lesson 8

    Make Claude yours

    Memory and preferences let Claude know your context so you repeat yourself less. Both are controlled in Settings, and what is available depends on your plan.

    Memory

    Claude can carry useful details from your chats into later ones, such as your role or ongoing projects. You control it in Settings, and you can ask Claude to remember or forget something.

    Remember that I prefer short answers with the recommendation first.

    Preferences

    Tell Claude how you like it to respond: tone, level of detail, formatting. They apply across chats.

    Explain things plainly. Skip long introductions. Use bullets only when I ask.

    Connectors, skills, and plugins

    These extend what Claude can reach and how it works. They have their own lessons, so this page stays short.

    Want a clean slate?Use an incognito chat, or turn off memory generation in Settings, and nothing is carried over from earlier chats.
    Lesson 9

    Plugins, connectors, skills, and MCP

    Four words that show up together. Connectors give Claude access to your tools. Skills teach it how you do a task. Plugins package both into one install. MCP is the standard underneath connectors.

    How the pieces fit

    One request, read in order
    You askin chat, the desktop app, or Claude Code
    Claude
    Plugin (optional)
    SkillYour steps, format, or checklist
    ConnectorA link to a service MCP server
    Your tools and datafiles, calendar, email, issues

    A skill gives Claude instructions it reads when your request needs them. A connector lets Claude read from and act in a service. A plugin is an optional wrapper that ships both, and sometimes more, in one install.

    PieceWhat it isUse it whenExample
    ConnectorA connection to a service MCP server, so Claude can read from it and act in it.Claude needs your tools or data.Your inbox, calendar, issue tracker, or an internal API
    SkillWritten instructions, sometimes with scripts and reference files, that Claude loads when a task calls for them.You want Claude to follow your process.A release-note format, a contract checklist, a weekly report
    PluginAn installable package that can hold skills, connectors, commands you run by name, and agents Claude hands work to.You want a ready-made setup, shared as one unit.Everything for one product, or your team standard setup
    MCPModel Context Protocol, a standard way for AI apps to reach tools and data.It sits under connectors, so you mostly meet it when adding a custom one.A remote MCP server address

    Try it: what do you need?

    Pick the situation closest to yours

    Add a plugin, step by step

    Paid plans: Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise
    1. Open Customize in the left sidebar, then the Plugins tab.
    2. Open Discover to browse available plugins.
    3. Select a plugin and click Add.
    4. Sign in to its connector from the plugin page, if it includes one.
    5. Use it. Type a slash or click the + in the message box to see the skills it adds. Some plugins also add commands you run by name.

    You can also add a custom plugin file or another marketplace. Source: Anthropic's help page on using plugins and the overview of connectors, skills, and plugins.

    Go deeper: where plugins work, and rules for teams
    Where they work

    Saved to your account

    Plugins, skills, and connectors you add in the web app or desktop app follow you to chat on web, desktop, and mobile, and to Claude Code when you sign in with the same account. Things added from the Claude Code command line stay on that computer.

    Where they work

    Chat versus longer tasks

    In chat, a plugin brings its skills, commands, and connectors. Longer task sessions in the desktop app and Claude Code also run its agents and hooks.

    Teams

    Owners set the rules

    On Team and Enterprise plans, Owners decide what members can add and share. Admins can require certain plugins and, on Enterprise, restrict which plugins and local MCP servers are allowed.

    MCP in plain words

    What a connector really is

    A service runs an MCP server that offers a list of tools, such as search, read, or create. A connector is Claude linked to that server. You sign in with the service, and your permission settings decide which tools Claude may use. Most people never touch MCP directly. You meet it when you add a custom connector by its server address, or when a developer builds one for a team tool.

    Go deeper: example tools and suggested settings
    Example toolConnectorWhat it doesSuggested setting
    get_messageGmailReads one emailAlways allow
    create_draftGmailSaves a draft without sending itNeeds approval
    forwardGmailSends a message on to someone elseNeeds approval
    delete_labelGmailRemoves a labelBlocked, if you never want it
    slack_read_threadSlackReads a threadAlways allow
    slack_create_canvasSlackCreates a canvas documentNeeds approval
    slack_send_messageSlackPosts a message others can seeNeeds approval

    Names vary by connector and can change over time. The suggested settings are a cautious starting point, not a rule.

    Trust before you connectA connector can read and act in a service on your behalf. Prefer Verified listings, add custom servers only from sources you trust, and keep anything that sends, posts, or deletes on Needs approval.
    Lesson 10

    Skills: teach Claude your way of doing things

    A skill is a short set of written instructions for one kind of task, such as your weekly report or your meeting notes. Claude uses it when a task calls for it, so you stop re-explaining the same steps.

    Skill, instructions, or memory?

    Pick the right tool
    ToolBest forExample
    A promptOne-off requests"Summarize this article in 3 bullets."
    Project instructionsBackground for one body of work"This project is our wedding. Budget is fixed."
    Preferences and memoryFacts about you, across all chats"Keep answers short, recommendation first."
    A skillA repeatable procedure with steps and a set output"Every Friday report: these sections, this order, this tone."

    Would a skill help?

    Tap a situation

    Try it: draft a skill

    Fill in the boxes, then copy the draft
    Skill draft

    Paste the draft into a chat and ask Claude to polish it, then add it under Customize, then Skills. Menu names and who can add skills depend on your plan, so check the help center if yours looks different.

    Worked example: a personal LinkedIn post from something you read

    Using a LinkedIn writing skill
    1. Find a skill. Open Customize, then Skills, and browse the skill directory for a LinkedIn or social-post writing skill. Check who published it before you add it. Directories and plan options differ, so if you cannot find one, use the Skill builder above to write your own.
    2. Turn it on and start a new chat. Claude will use the skill when you ask for a LinkedIn post.
    3. Bring your source. Paste your own notes or a short summary of the book, blog post, or news story. For a book, use your highlights, not whole chapters.
    4. Add the personal part. This is what makes the post sound like you: where you saw the idea in your own work, or what changed your mind.
    5. Ask for a draft, then edit it in your own voice. You review it and post it yourself.

    Try it. Pick what you read, then fill in the boxes.

    Ask Claude

    What a good draft sounds likeA short opening line that makes someone stop scrolling. Then the idea in one or two sentences, your own moment ("last month I..."), one takeaway, and a closing question. About 120 to 200 words, with no buzzwords.
    Keep it honest

    Do not let Claude invent your story

    Give it a true detail, even a small one. If you leave it out, the post turns generic. Check any quote or number against the source.

    Good habit

    Name the source

    Credit the author or link the article. Summarize in your own words rather than copying passages.

    Already built in

    File skills

    Claude already has skills for making Word documents, PowerPoint decks, Excel sheets, and PDFs, which is why it can hand you finished files.

    Tips for good skills

    • One skill, one job
    • Say when it should be used
    • Describe the finished result, not only the steps
    • Test it on a small example first

    Skills and plugins

    A plugin can bundle several skills with connectors so a whole team installs them together.

    Lesson 11

    Connect Gmail, GitHub, Slack, and more

    Connectors let Claude read from the apps where your work lives and, with your approval, act in them. Instead of pasting an email thread into the chat, you connect Gmail once and ask for a summary of the thread about the venue contract.

    Add a connector, step by step

    Same flow for most services
    1. Open Customize, then Connectors. In the desktop app, choose Customize in the sidebar. Menu names can change, so search the help center if yours looks different.
    2. Find the service. Browse the directory or search by name, such as Gmail, GitHub, or Slack. Check whether a listing is marked Verified or Community.
    3. Click to connect. Some services first ask for a server address or your account region. On Team or Enterprise plans, an Owner may need to add the connector for your organization first.
    4. Sign in and approve. You log in on the service's own page and approve the access it lists. Claude never sees your password.
    5. Check the status. The connector should show as Connected.
    6. Turn it on in a chat. Click the + in the message box, choose Connectors, and switch it on for this conversation. Then ask for something that needs the app.
    7. Set permissions. On the connector's page, set each group of tools to Always allow, Needs approval, or Blocked.

    Source: Anthropic's help pages on getting started with connectors and custom connectors.

    Try it: pick a service

    See what it unlocks and what to ask

    Combine apps in one request

    Once two are connected
    Morning prep

    Check my calendar for tomorrow. For each meeting, find the most recent related email thread and give me a two-line summary and one question I should be ready to answer.

    Engineering digest

    List the pull requests merged this week, then search the #engineering channel for related discussion. Write a short digest grouped by theme. Show it to me before posting anything.

    Meeting follow-up

    Find the planning doc from last week's meeting, pull out the action items with owners, and draft a follow-up email to the attendees. Save it as a draft and do not send it.

    Rule of thumb: let reading run, keep anything that sends, posts, or changes on Needs approval, and block what you never want. Lesson 9 has a table of example tools with suggested settings.

    Treat what Claude reads as dataAn email, web page, or document can contain text that tries to give Claude orders. If Claude points out an instruction inside such content, or asks to do something you did not request, decline.

    When something goes wrong

    ProblemWhat to try
    Can't find the serviceSearch by name. On a work plan, ask your Owner to add it. If the tool offers a connection address (called a remote MCP server), you can add it as a custom connector.
    Connected, but Claude doesn't use itOpen the + menu in the chat, choose Connectors, and switch it on for this conversation.
    It shows ReconnectAccess lapsed. Click Reconnect and sign in again.
    You want Claude to stop using itTurning off the chat toggle only pauses it. Use Disconnect to revoke access, or Remove to delete the connector.
    Claude keeps asking for approvalSet that group of tools to Always allow if it only reads. Keep sending and changing tools on Needs approval.

    Custom connectors are in beta and work with servers you enter by address. Only add servers you trust, and review which tools you allow.

      Lesson 12

      Organize files and automate tasks

      With the Claude desktop app, Claude can work on folders on your computer: sort and rename files, build an index, write a report. It can also repeat a job for you on a schedule. What is available depends on your plan and settings.

      How a folder job runs

      You decide what Claude can reach
      1. Open the chat in the desktop app on the computer that has the files.
      2. Connect a folder. Claude can only see the folders you choose.
      3. Ask for a plan first. Have Claude list what it would change before it changes anything.
      4. Approve, then let it work. Look over the result when it finishes.
      Built-in care

      New files first

      Claude saves results next to your originals and changes an existing file only when you ask it to.

      Built-in care

      Deleting needs your OK

      Claude asks before it deletes anything. If you would rather not allow that, it moves files into a _to_delete folder for you to review and empty yourself.

      Good to know

      Your computer must be reachable

      If the computer is asleep, offline, or the app is closed, Claude can't reach the folder. You can attach files to the chat instead.

      Lesson 14
      
          
      Delegate: hand off a big job
      
          
      Beyond chat, Claude can take on a multi-step job, work through it on its own, and come back with finished files. You describe the outcome, check in when you like, and review the result.
      
        
      

        
      
          
      How a hand-off runs
      You stay in charge
      
          
        
            
      1. You describe the outcome. Say what you want at the end, not each click along the way.
        2. 
            
      2. Claude says what it is about to do and sets up a task list, so you can see what is done and what is left.
        3. 
            
      3. It works through the steps using the tools you have allowed, such as search, files, and connected apps. It may pause to ask for approval.
        4. 
            
      4. It checks its work, then hands you the finished file or answer with a short summary.
        5. 
            
      5. If you step away, Claude takes the most reasonable reading of your request and notes that choice at the top of its work, so you can correct it.
        6. 
          
      
        
      

        
      
          
      Try it: write a hand-off brief
      Pick an example or fill in your own
      
          
      
          
      
            
            
            
            
            
          
      
          
      Hand-off brief
      
        
      

        
      
          
      What to hand off, and what to keep
      A simple rule of thumb
      
          
      
            
      Good to hand offBetter to keep yourself
      
            
              
      Research that needs many sources and a written summaryFinal decisions with real consequences
      
              
      Turning rough notes into a deck or reportAnything you cannot check afterwards
      
              
      Sorting and renaming files, with a plan firstSending messages or payments on your behalf without review
      
              
      Repeat jobs that follow the same steps each timeTasks where the goal is still fuzzy
      
                  
          
      
        
      

        
      Stay safeStart with tasks that read and write new files. Keep approvals on for anything that sends, deletes, or changes things in your apps, and review the result before you rely on it.

      Lesson
      
          
      Alerts: warn people before something expires
      
          
      Contracts, certificates, licenses, and targets all have dates. Claude can read your tracker, work out how many days are left, sort each item into an amber or red bucket, and prepare one email per owner.
      
        
      

        
      
          
      Can it be done?
      Short answer: yes, with a few conditions
      
          
      
            
      Where the dates liveWhat works
      
            
              
      An Excel file in a folder on your computerYes. In the Claude desktop app, a scheduled task can read the file each time it runs. Your computer needs to be on and the app open.
      
              
      An Excel file in SharePoint or OneDriveThe Microsoft 365 connector can search these. Check that it can read the cells you need. If not, keep a copy in a connected folder.
      
              
      A Tableau dashboardI did not find a Tableau connector in the directory. Use Tableau's own data alerts and subscriptions, or export the underlying data to Excel or CSV on a schedule and let Claude read that.
      
              
      The emails themselvesWith the Gmail connector Claude can write drafts. Whether it can also send depends on your connector and permissions. The safest setup is draft first, or send only with your approval.
      
                  
          
      
          
      For alerts that must never be missed, such as a legal deadline, use a dedicated alerting tool as the main system (Tableau alerts, Excel with Power Automate, or your calendar) and let Claude be the helper that checks and writes the messages.
      
        
      

        
      
          
      Try it: a sample expiry tracker
      Change the date or the limits and watch the buckets move
      
          
      
            
            
            
          
      
          
      
            
      ItemOwnerExpiresDays leftBucket
      
            
          
      
          
      
        
      

        
      
          
      The emails Claude would prepare
      One per owner, grouped by urgency
      
          
      
          
      
        
      

        
      
          
      The rules, in plain words
      Say these in your prompt
      
          
      
            
      BucketWhenWhat happens
      
            
              
      ExpiredDate has passedTell the owner and their manager
      
              
      Red30 days or fewerUrgent email to the owner
      
              
      Amber31 to 45 daysHeads-up email to the owner
      
              
      GreenMore than 45 daysNo email
      
                  
          
      
          
      Add a "Last alerted" column. Ask Claude to email each item once when it enters amber and once when it enters red, so owners are not reminded every week about the same thing.
      
        
      

        
      
          
      Set it up
      Five steps
      
          
        
            
      1. Make the sheet clean. One row per item, with columns for item, owner, owner email, expiry date, and last alerted. Dates must be real dates, not text.
        2. 
            
      2. Connect the folder that holds it in the Claude desktop app, and connect your email app.
        3. 
            
      3. Do a dry run. Ask Claude to show the buckets and the emails it would write, and send nothing.
        4. 
            
      4. Set it as a scheduled task, with emails left as drafts until you trust it.
        5. 
            
      5. Review the first few runs, then decide whether to let it send with your approval.
        6. 
          
      
          
      Prompt for a scheduled task
      
        
      

        
      
          
      Safe habit
      Dry run first
      Always see the list and the emails before anything goes to real people. Fix the sheet, then switch on the schedule.
      
          
      Know this
      Each run starts fresh
      A scheduled run has no memory of this chat. The prompt must name the file, the limits, and what to do if something looks wrong.
      
          
      Privacy
      Check who gets what
      Emails should go only to the owner in the row, with only their items. Keep email addresses in the sheet accurate.
      
        
      
        
      
      
      

      
      
        
      
          
      Lesson
      
          
      Compare two Excel files and highlight the mismatches
      
          
      Two versions of the same list never quite agree. Claude can read both files, match the rows, compare every cell, and give you a new workbook that shows exactly what differs, without touching either original.
      
        
      

        
      
          
      Can it be done?
      Yes. Here is what Claude does
      
          
        
            
      1. Reads both files and checks the columns, the sheets, and how dates and numbers are stored.
        2. 
            
      2. Matches rows by a key, such as an invoice number or an employee ID. Without a key, row 5 is compared to row 5, which breaks as soon as one file has an extra row.
        3. 
            
      3. Compares cell by cell and sorts the results into changed values, rows only in the first file, and rows only in the second.
        4. 
            
      4. Builds a new workbook with a summary, a list of differences, and copies of both sheets with mismatches highlighted. Your originals stay untouched.
        5. 
          
      
        
      

        
      
          
      Try it: compare two invoice lists
      Change the rules and watch the mismatches change
      
          
      File A is an export from the accounting system. File B is a copy kept by finance. Both should say the same thing.
      
          
      
            
            
          
      
          
      
            
      File A: accounting-export.xlsx
      
            
      File B: finance-copy.xlsx
      
          
      
          
      
          
      The Differences tab
      
          
      InvoiceWhat differsFile AFile B
      
        
      

        
      
          
      What the report workbook contains
      A new file, next to your originals
      
          
      Summary · counts and rules usedDifferences · one line per mismatchOnly in AOnly in BA highlighted · copy of AB highlighted · copy of B
      
          
      Highlighted cells also carry a note or a marker, so the report still makes sense when printed in black and white.
      
        
      

        
      
          
      Ask Claude
      Attach both files with the + button first
      
          
      Prompt
      
          
      Not sure which column is the key? Ask first: "Look at both files and suggest a column that uniquely identifies each row. Do not compare yet."
      
        
      

        
      
          
      Choose the key with care
      It must be unique in both files. Customer name is a poor key because it repeats. Ask Claude to report any duplicate keys.
      
          
      Decide what counts as a difference
      Capital letters, trailing spaces, date formats, and tiny rounding gaps are usually noise. Say which ones to ignore, as in the demo above.
      
          
      Values, not formulas
      By default Claude compares what the cells show. If you need formulas compared, say so. Also mention hidden sheets or merged cells.
      
        
      
        
      Before you rely on itSpot check a few flagged rows against the original files, and a few unflagged ones too. For very large files, compare one sheet or one date range first. Your originals are never edited unless you ask.
      
        
      
      
      

      
      
        
      
          
      Lesson
      
          
      Team: a daily list, stand-up and activity report
      
          
      Start with a simple daily to-do list with ticks. Then grow it into a shared sheet that a team uses for stand-up, and that adds up everything done by day, week, month and year: issues raised, closed and escalated, bulletins sent, and the projects worked on. No plugin is needed, only a chat and a spreadsheet.
      
        
      

        
      
          
      Step 1: a daily list in a chat
      Say your tasks out loud
      
          
      Priya runs a small bakery. Each morning she types her tasks the way she would say them. Claude returns a checklist. Try ticking the sample below.
      
          
      Prompt
      Make me a to-do list for today, Wednesday 7 Oct, as a checklist I can tick. Tasks: confirm the Saturday wedding cake order, buy flour and butter, pay the electricity bill, reply to the cafe about Friday's delivery, post this week's special on Instagram, clean the oven. Mark the cake order and the bill as high priority. Show a progress bar and a Done and Pending count.
      
          
      
            Sample: tick the boxes
            
      Wednesday, 7 Oct
      
            
      
            
      6Total
      0Done
      0Pending
      
            
        
            
        
          
        
          
        At six o'clock, tell Claude what you finished: “I did the cake order, the flour and butter, the cafe reply and the Instagram post.” It writes an end-of-day report (4 of 6 done, 67%) and carries the rest to tomorrow with the high-priority bill at the top. The next morning, say “New day. Start from yesterday's pending items and add…”
        
        
        

        
        
          
        Step 2: at work, add tasks by project
        Projects and ad hoc tasks
        
          
        Work days differ. Give every task a project name, and add new projects or one-off tasks whenever they appear.
        
          
        Prompt
        Today, Wednesday 7 Oct. Website relaunch: review homepage mockups (high priority). Q4 budget: collect team forecasts (high priority). Client onboarding: schedule the kickoff call (high) and send the welcome pack. Admin: approve timesheets. Make me a checklist grouped by project with tick boxes.
        
          
        What comes back (illustrative)
        Website relaunch
        ☐ Review homepage mockups (high)
        Q4 budget
        ☐ Collect team forecasts (high)
        Client onboarding
        ☐ Schedule kickoff call (high)
        ☐ Send welcome pack
        Admin
        ☐ Approve timesheets
        
          
        
            
        A new project
        Say “New project: Office move. Add: get three removal quotes (high priority).” In the sheet, type the name on the Projects tab and it appears in the Project dropdown.
        
            
        An ad hoc task
        Say “Unplanned: the boss wants a quick report by 3 pm.” In the sheet, set Type to Unplanned and use the Ad hoc project if it belongs to none. Later ask how much of your week was unplanned.
        
          
        
        
        

        
        
          
        Step 3: keep it all year in Google Sheets
        Two records, nine tabs
        
          
        A chat is good for today. For a year, a spreadsheet keeps every day, saves automatically, and adds things up for you. Google Sheets lets several people edit at once and works on a phone. The sheet keeps two kinds of record, because they answer different questions.
        
          
        RecordIt answersExample row
        
            
        Daily (planned work)What is on, what is done, what is blocked?Test checkout flow, Ben, Blocked: waiting for sandbox access
        
            
        Log (what we did)How many issues did we raise, close or escalate? How many bulletins went out?Anita, Website relaunch, Issue closed, INC-1063
        
          
        
          
        Stand-up · done, today, blockedReport · day, week, month, yearWeekly · all 53 weeksBreakdown · by person and projectDaily · planned tasksLog · what we didPeopleProjectsLists · activity types
        
        
        

        
        
          
        Track all the work: issues and bulletins
        One row each time something is done
        
          
        Whenever someone raises an issue, closes one, escalates one or sends a bulletin, they add one row to the Log. That is all the team has to do. The Report tab adds it up.
        
          
        The Log tab (sample rows)

        Activity is a dropdown. The four starting types are Issue raised, Issue closed, Issue escalated and Bulletin sent. Add your own, such as Customer call, on the Lists tab (up to 8). They become new columns on the Report.

        Your team routine
        About five minutes before stand-up
        
          
          
            
        1. Before stand-up: each person updates their Daily rows (Status, Blocker note, Done on) and adds Log rows for issues and bulletins since yesterday.
          2. 
            
        2. In stand-up: open the Stand-up tab on a shared screen. Go through Blocked first, then Doing today, and skim Done.
          3. 
            
        3. After stand-up: add new or unplanned tasks (set Type to Unplanned) and give each blocker to someone who can clear it.
          4. 
            
        4. Friday: open the Report tab, check the week's totals, and send the weekly bulletin.
          5. 
            
        5. Month end and year end: read the month and year rows, then ask Claude what changed and why.
          6. 
          
        
        
        

        
        
          
        Get the starter file
        A team of four, with sample data
        
          
        An Excel file with all nine tabs, the formulas, dropdowns for Project, Owner, Type, Status and Activity, and the sample data above (343 tasks and 159 log entries over five weeks). Upload it to Google Drive, right-click it and choose Open with Google Sheets. Delete the sample rows (keep row 1), then type your team on the People tab and your projects on the Projects tab.
        
          
        
          
        If a download is blocked where you are viewing this page, ask Claude to build the file for you in a chat.
        
        
        

        
        
          
        Ask Claude
        Paste the tab you want summarised
        
          
        Prompt
        Here is the Report tab. Write a short monthly summary for my manager: issues raised vs closed, how many were escalated, bulletins sent, and anything that stands out.
        
          
        Prompt
        Here is the Stand-up tab. Write a five-line stand-up summary for the team channel and flag the three biggest risks.
        
          
        Prompt
        Which blockers have been open more than two working days, and who could clear each one?
        
          
        Prompt
        Here are the notes from today's stand-up. List the actions agreed, who owns each, and the date.
        
        
        

        
        
          
        Room to grow
        Daily and Log each hold 10,000 rows, about three years of tasks at this team's pace. Stand-up lists up to 40 done, 40 for today and 25 blocked, and shows the full count. People holds 25 names, Projects 50, Lists 8 activity types. To go further, copy the formulas down or start a fresh file each year and keep the old one as the archive.
        
          
        It is only as complete as the rows
        The numbers are only as good as what the team adds. Agree on a rule, such as logging before the stand-up.
        
          
        Sharing and privacy
        Several people can edit one Google Sheet only if it is shared with edit access. Check your company's rules on where project data may be stored before you share it.
        
        
        
        
        Before you rely on itThe Report, Weekly, Breakdown, Stand-up, People and Projects formulas were checked against an independent count, for Everyone and for one person on one project, and matched. The dropdowns are validation rules carried over from Excel, so check them once in Google Sheets. A file this size can take a few seconds to recalculate. The stand-up date is fixed at 7 Oct in the sample; type =TODAY() into it for live use. Claude cannot create the sheet in your Google account unless Google Drive is connected, so you upload the file yourself.

        Lesson 16
        
          
        Using Claude well
        
          
        A few habits separate people who get steady value from people who get stuck.
        
        
        
        
        
          
        If this happensTry this
        
          
            
        The answer is genericAdd context, audience, and a format. Use the Prompt Lab pieces from lesson 2.
        
            
        The answer is too longSet a length: "under 100 words" or "3 bullets".
        
            
        Claude misunderstood youSay what was wrong, then restate the goal. Or ask "what did you assume?"
        
            
        You doubt a factAsk for sources, turn on search, and check the original.
        
            
        A long chat gets muddled, or you change topicsSummarize and start a new chat. Lesson 3 explains why.
        
          
        
        
        
          
        Verify what matters
        Claude can be confidently wrong. Check figures, quotes, and citations before you use them, and get professional advice for legal, medical, and financial decisions.
        
          
        Protect sensitive data
        Don't paste passwords, payment details, or private information about other people unless you have a good reason and the right to share it.
        
          
        Give feedback
        The thumbs up and thumbs down buttons on a response tell Anthropic what worked and what didn't.
        
        
        
        
        Help articles live at support.claude.com, and developers can start at docs.claude.com.
